questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalue that Corresponds to a Given Eigenvector
questions.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}15 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-3)\cdot [\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=-3v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3.$

questions.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

If $v$ is an eigenvector, then there must exist a real number $\lambda $ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ Hence, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=\lambda [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

This leads to the following system of equations for $\lambda :$

$$
{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda  \\ -2=-\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

This system has no solution. Therefore, $v$ is not an eigenvector of $A.$

questions.problem: The eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}k & -1 \\ 2 & 2k\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =k+2$ is  $[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ k-1\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}k & -1 \\ 2 & 2k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ k-1\end{aligned}] & =(k+2)[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ k-1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-2k+1 \\ -2+2{k}^{2}-2k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-k-2 \\ {k}^{2}+k-2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2k+1=-k-2, \\ -2+2{k}^{2}-2k={k}^{2}+k-2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
-k=-3\,⟹\,k=3.
$$

Now, substituting $k=3$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2+2{k}^{2}-2k & ={k}^{2}+k-2 \\ -2+2\cdot (3)^{2}-2\cdot 3 & =(3)^{2}+3-2 \\ 10 & =10,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=3.$

questions.problem: An eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}11 & -6 \\ -12 & 25\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ is  $v=[\begin{aligned}c+1 \\ c\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $c.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}11 & -6 \\ -12 & 25\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}c+1 \\ c\end{aligned}] & =7[\begin{aligned}c+1 \\ c\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5c+11 \\ 13c-12\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7c+7 \\ 7c\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}5c+11=7c+7 \\ 13c-12=7c\end{aligned}
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the first equation, we get

$$
5c+11=7c+7\,⟹\,c=2.
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the second equation, we get

$$
13c-12=7c\,⟹\,c=2.
$$

Therefore, the solution of the system is $c=2.$

questions.problem: The eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -8+k \\ 3 & 5k\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2k$ is  $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -8+k \\ 3 & 5k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =2k[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}k-10 \\ -6+5k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4k \\ 2k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}k-10=-4k, \\ -6+5k=2k\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
k-10=-4k\,⟹\,k=2.
$$

Now, substituting $k=2$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6+5k & =2k \\ -6+5(2) & =2(2) \\ 4 & =4,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=2.$

questions.problem: The eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 20-4k & 3\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2k+1$ is  $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 20-4k & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =(2k+1)[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 26-4k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2k+1 \\ 4k+2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}7=2k+1, \\ 26-4k=4k+2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
7=2k+1\,⟹\,k=3.
$$

Now, substituting $k=3$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}26-4k & =4k+2 \\ 26-4\cdot 3 & =4\cdot 3+2 \\ 14 & =14,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $v$ is an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\frac{1}{7}$ then $v$ is also an eigenvector of the matrix ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =7.$
- An eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ is also an eigenvector of the inverse ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =1.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\frac{1}{2},$ then $-v$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=\frac{1}{7}v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=\frac{1}{7}{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $7$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=7v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector  of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $7.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is false. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =\frac{1}{-1}=-1.$

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(-v)=-Av=-(\frac{1}{2}v)=\frac{1}{2}(-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(-v)=\frac{1}{2}(-v),$ and $-v\ne 0,$ this implies that $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $2.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ then $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=2v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2.$

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(-v)=-Av=-(2v)=2(-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(-v)=2(-v),$ and $-v\ne 0,$ this implies that $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2$ (but not $-2$).

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

- Statement III is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =0[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =0v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=0v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

- $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ then $3v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-6.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =1$ (but not $-1$).

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =-3\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=-3v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3.$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(3v)=3Av=3(-2v)=-2(3v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(3v)=-2(3v),$ and $3v\ne 0,$ this implies that $3v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (but not $-6$).

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Value of an Unknown Given an Eigenvalue and Eigenvector of a Matrix
canonical_examples.problem: An eigenvector of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071103/assets/f5ac973d5d7dd390f8cf9231515815f334d0c01dafeab14ba58fef25db4a8e8d.png) corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda=6c$ is  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071103/assets/a7e303f19be04db829faaa41133c70d7b6e5647ed75063674ca564a2952c09eb.png) Determine the value of $c.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2c\end{aligned}] & =6c[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2c\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2+2c \\ 1+4c\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6c \\ 12{c}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2+2c=6c \\ 1+4c=12{c}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $c$ in the first equation, we get

$$
2+2c=6c \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad c = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, substituting $c=\dfrac{1}{2}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+4c & =12{c}^{2} \\ 1+4\cdot \frac{1}{2} & =12{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ 3 & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solutions of the system is $c=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071103/assets/f35353367a395e7b3560aa6f7ef0da0936cefbced9e76d6d7d8f91426a7a1c9b.png) is an eigenvector of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071103/assets/0b4f33107845bf52d80802844bc6faaec6ab9f4bd159a87838497d2f6abe72d1.png) that corresponds to the eigenvalue $2.$

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071103/assets/ea0bc4d487e57434694dac1835e082f63c9467b496933c8e36770334e77713f5.png) is an eigenvector of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071103/assets/c87d5c13bbd73d56f44af3ec1b4a867c86e8bf4f709fa869ab8d142424cbe8c4.png) that corresponds to the eigenvalue $0.$

- If $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = 5,$ then $2\mathbf{v}$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda = 5.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A\mathbf{v}=2 \mathbf{v},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda=2.$

- Statement II is false. An eigenvector must be a *non-zero* vector.

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(2v)=2Av=2(5v)=5(2v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(2\mathbf{v})=5( 2 \mathbf{v} ),$ and $2 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0},$ this implies that $2 \mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda = 5.$

Therefore, the correct answer is, "I and III only."

**Note:** Statement III is true in the general case, too. In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.
